t: K-th Largest Perfect Subtree Size — Post-Order Verification
o: A perfect binary subtree has all leaves at one depth and every internal node with two children. Collect the sizes of all perfect subtrees and report the k-th largest, or -1 if fewer than k exist. In example 1 the sizes sorted descending are [3,3,1,1,1,1,1,1], so k=2 gives 3. A post-order DFS decides perfection bottom-up: a node roots a perfect subtree of size l+r+1 iff both children root perfect subtrees of equal size.
k: A node is a perfect-subtree root iff both children are perfect roots with equal subtree sizes.
Returning -1 (or 0) as a sentinel for 'not perfect' propagates failure up the recursion in O(1) per node.

a.i: Post-order DFS returns the subtree size when perfect and -1 otherwise. Append each perfect size to a list, sort descending, and index k-1. With at most 2000 nodes this is far within limits.
s: dfs(node): l = dfs(left), r = dfs(right); if l < 0 or r < 0 or l != r return -1, else record s = l+r+1 and return s.
Sort sizes descending; return sizes[k-1] if it exists else -1.
a.t: O(n log n) — O(n) DFS plus sorting up to n collected sizes.
a.sp: O(n) — sizes list and recursion stack.

a.n: Approach 2: DFS + Min-Heap of Size k
a.i: Instead of sorting everything, keep a min-heap holding the k largest sizes seen; each leaf-to-root pass pushes the size and pops when the heap exceeds k. The heap root is then the k-th largest, using O(k) extra memory — useful when k << n.
s: On each perfect subtree of size s: push s; if |h| > k, pop the minimum.
After the DFS, return h[0] if |h| == k else -1.
a.t: O(n log k) — DFS is O(n); each of the ≤ n recorded sizes costs O(log k) heap work.
a.sp: O(k + h) — heap of size k plus O(height) recursion stack.

w: Either approach is interview-safe; mention the heap variant if asked about memory. Pitfalls: a node with one child is never perfect (the -1 sentinel handles it), and sizes must be recorded for every perfect node, not just maximal ones — leaves count as size-1 perfect subtrees. Follow-up: count perfect subtrees of each possible size, or do it iteratively without recursion.
